lines.text: How does a beetle shoot boiling liquid out of its rear without cooking itself?
This is a bombardier beetle, and when something attacks, it blasts an irritating spray right back.
That spray comes out almost at boiling, around one hundred degrees Celsius.
Inside, a pouch stores the ingredients, and a tiny chamber holds special enzymes.
When danger shows up, it lets some into the chamber, and the mix reacts in a burst of heat.
That heat makes steam, and the pressure fires the spray out of its tail.
In 2015, scientists filmed this inside living beetles with X-rays, and here's the twist.
It's not one long squirt. It's hundreds of tiny blasts, up to about five hundred every second.
Scientists think the pulsing lets the chamber cool between blasts, and the chamber walls are extra tough.
So it only makes its boiling weapon at the exact moment it needs it.
Would you dare pick one up?
